review:
I am FAR away from being the most knowledgeable person when it come to this series but I do earnestly think this is a very, VERY fun traditional base building rts game.

While I have yet to play a PVP match or any of the campaigns, I have gotten over 30 hours of playtime from "skirmish" and "comp stomp" matches alone in a little over 2 weeks.
Things I particularly like about AoE2DE at the moment include the way the game structures its factions, the soundtrack of the game and some specific factions I have grown to like (Namely The Sicilians and Hindustanis).

On the other hand, things I dislike about the game largely include things that can be chalked up to skill-issues(Feeling stressed from having a bunch of enemies in your base, having your invasion force killed off easily, etc). I will also note that -> from what I've seen <-, getting all the faction adding DLCs so that you have everything at your disposal for ranked play is a fairly expensive endeavor.

In conclusion, I really like this game and I will try to remember to update my review of it after I get some hands on experience with the PVP (Maybe including some ranked 1v1's) and campaigns of this game.

I would like to preface this by saying I love Age of Empires 2. It's my favorite RTS, and one of the best games of all time. The Definitive Edition is arguably the best way to play it

That said, I hate how fragile the multiplayer is. It's not possible to re-join a game. This affects team games the most because if a player drops, their team will likely lose

This was acceptable in 1999 - friends were playing via LAN. If someone dropped, they could use the "restore game" function

It doesn't work in 2026 - strangers are playing via modern matchmaking, if someone drops, they just continue playing

It takes one disconnect to lose a 3 hour team game. It doesn't help that the game is prone to crashes

As far as I understand DE is based on the original code from 1999. The developers did a great job modernizing most parts. But the multiplayer is just not up to modern standards

PS: please fix shift queuing walls

This is the quintessential game for fans of Real-Time Strategy. While definitely an old classic, the newer expansions released in the past few years, Three Kingdoms, Last Chieftains, and The Viking Sagas, have shown that the game is still evolving over time, with old civilizations never being forgotten, and newer ones continuing to find ways to stay unique while keeping the same core principles as the other civilizations. For fans of history of all time periods, from the Fall of Babylon to the Sacking of Rome by the Visigoths and Vandals, the Battle of Hastings, the Mongol Conquests, and the rise of Poland and the Safavids, you'll find plenty of unique campaigns to fill that love of history for hundreds of hours.

I am reviewing this from a strictly single player perspective, please keep that in mind.
That being said, I do not recommend this game for someone seeking a good single player RTS.
- The AI can outpace that player at every step of the way.
The first few missions in the first starter campaign are fine, but as soon as you step out of that one the AI is suddenly that same thing 90% of RTS are that focus more on single player. 
- "Rush the player" constantly is such an over used tactic for weak AI. You can't sit back and enjoy getting your civilization up and running because the enemy AI just keeps attacking, attacking, attacking and soon you find yourself spending 80% of your time defending yourself, repairing damage then trying to get back to setting up a farm.  I don't see how this is enjoyable from a single player perspective.
- Even if you focus on defense from the start, you are still running against the clock of "how soon will the enemy send an annoying force that I have to prepare for.
- I get this a "war" based game, but when a human being has to jungle 30 different things at once when the AI can do the same thing in 0.5 seconds it because a game of frustration rather than strategy or tactics.
- The only tactic that works at is to focus purely on military and quickly overwhelm the enemy with a massive force. How is that "strategy" when it's just "how fast can you click".

I know I'm going to be the odd man out on my review, and that's fine, but there are some of us who love the setting and the idea of bringing up your civilization AND having military conflict, but this game seems to only care about the military part and all the other stuff is just window dressing.

And before someone yells at me "this game is for multiplayer, yeah I get that, but it is sold and listened as single player as well, why bother with single player campaigns then?

Functionally the game runs great, looks good and is pretty bug free, gameplay wise, it's just not enjoyable.

Do you have limited free time that you would like to give up? Do you like to to play a game the right way then go back through with cheats and steam roll NPC's? Do you want your wife to give you weird looks while you sit on your laptop and play at the kitchen table? If so, I have a game for you!

Look. I know pointing to my playtime and walking away is lazy, but like...what more do you want from me? It's the 1999 classic in all its glory but with a support level on par with any modern game. You can reasonably criticize the idea to upend certain long-standing gameplay systems with more recent patches and expansions, but at its core it still hits all the nostalgia notes while also allowing the growth that comes from 25+ years of game and map design evolution. And some of the newer, longer story campaigns from Chronicles or the recent Viking Sagas show that the underlying engine can power vastly different ideas than whatever was envisioned back then.

Like, I can play a complicated, 12-hour scenario full of triggers and conditions, with all the polish of a major studio, but I can also still play basically the same scenarios I played on my Pentium III when I was 15. Or I can just comp-stomp and vibe to the soundtrack. More than any of the other Definitive Editions, it's a platform for both memories and modern development.
